title: Falling wedge on a small cap after a failed pump. Do you trust these?
author: FarInspector1873
selftext:
GTC/USDT, 1h chart (Oct 24–26).

It spiked hard on Oct 25 around midnight, with a wick toward 0.30 on about 50M volume. It gave the whole move back within hours and has since bled into a narrowing wedge. Price is now around 0.226, pressed between a steep falling top line and a shallower bottom line, and it's getting close to the apex.

What bugs me:

* Only 2 touches on each line, so the wedge is technically valid but not very convincing.
* Volume has been drying up inside the wedge, which fits the pattern, but the earlier spike makes me doubt it.
* Wedges this far into the apex tend to break soon, and the direction isn't guaranteed.

I'd want to see a clean hourly close outside the upper line before treating this as anything. Until then it's just a chart to watch.

How do you handle wedges on lower-cap coins after a pump and dump? Do you trade them, or ignore them until there are more touches?

Not advice, just sharing what I'm watching.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: two touches a side on the 1h after a pump that gave everything back, I wouldn't trust it. drying volume fits a wedge, but it also fits nobody caring about the coin anymore.

replies.author: FarInspector1873
replies.body: Agreed, two touches isn't much. Volume on the breakout candle is the only thing that would change my mind, since drying volume alone can't separate a wedge from a dead coin.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: yeah, volume on the break is the only tell worth waiting for there. a thin breakout on a name that already failed one pump mostly gets sold into.

comments.author: RobodOfficial
comments.body: Your point about the earlier spike matters more than adding another trendline touch. A wedge after a full pump retracement may behave differently from one in an established uptrend. A useful test would separate those two groups, define the hourly-close breakout rule beforehand, and track how often price falls back inside the wedge. Include spread and slippage too, since a small-cap breakout can look much cleaner on candles than in actual fills.

replies.author: FarInspector1873
replies.body: Good points. The failed-breakout rate and real fill quality would tell me more than the pattern itself. Do you have a go to way of modelling slippage on thin pairs?

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Waiting for a clean close outside the line is a sensible rule, and noticing the thin touch count is the right instinct. On small caps after a pump the pattern is noisy, because one big wick can distort both lines and the spread is wider when you exit. I'd look at how past wedges on this coin behaved, counting the failures too, and size small until a breakout comes with real volume. Cymetica's Backtest Labs can test a rule like "buy the close above the wedge" on past data with fees included.
